articles.title: Trump administration has pushed off 13% of Americans enrolled in food stamps
articles.summary: Stakeholders concerned more people at risk of food insecurity after One Big Beautiful Act took effect
articles.body:
Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) has decreased significantly over the past year in the US following restrictions imposed by the Trump administration, which has forced more people to seek help from food banks or go hungry, stakeholders say.

The number of people who receive food stamps has dropped from 41.6 million in July 2025, before the One Big Beautiful Act took effect, to 36.5 million in June 2026, a 13% decrease, according to the latest data from the US Department of Agriculture , which administers the program.

While Donald Trump and other Republicans have said the changes incentivize people to find jobs, elected officials, non-profit leaders and people with food insecurity say the changes simply make it harder for Americans to feed their families.

"There is always going to be a percentage of our communities who we need to help – we have to accept that – and so, once we accept it, it is easy to just move forward and do the right thing, which is to provide resources to people who need them," said Rhona Kamar, founder and executive director of Feed Louisville, a non-profit that aims to reduce hunger and food waste.

The Trump administration's changes to Snap will reduce spending by about $187bn over 10 years, the congressional budget office projected .

Previously, only able-bodied people between ages 18 and 54 who did not have dependents under 18 had to meet a requirement that they work a minimum of 20 hours per week or only get benefits for a maximum of three months over three years.

Under Trump, the rules now state that people from ages 18 to 64 who do not have a dependent under 14 had to perform paid or volunteer work for at least 20 hours weekly.

The One Big Beautiful Act also stated that starting October, states had to cover 75% of the Snap administrative costs, whereas before they had to cover half.

The changes have affected some states more than others. In Arizona, the number of people enrolled in Snap dropped by 50% between July 2025 and June 2026; Kentucky experienced a 6% decrease.

"I am concerned more people are going hungry in my state because of changes to" Snap, "impacting children and the elderly", Kentucky governor, Andy Beshear, a Democrat who leads the predominantly Republican state, stated in a letter this month to Brooke Rollins, the US agriculture secretary.

But Trump and Rollins described the reduction in Snap recipients as a positive.

"Democrats don't love" the decrease, Rollins said at a farming festival in August in Minnesota. "But for those of us that love work and celebrate work and want people to work and not be on food stamps, it's a pretty big win when we move 5 million people off of food stamps."

Critics of the changes point out that despite Trump's promises, grocery and gas prices have increased during his second term, making it harder for families to afford necessities.

"If people were getting paid enough, they would not be on the Snap program," said Gina Plata-Nino, director of Snap at the Food Research and Action Center, a non-profit that supports anti-hunger programs.

The Food Bank Council of Michigan operates a helpline where staff answer residents' questions about applying for Snap and accessing local food programs. The organization started getting more than three times as many calls daily after the Snap changes took effect. This week, they had to temporarily suspend the helpline because of the high call volume.

The changes have also affected Feed Louisville, which receives surplus food from restaurants and farmers and uses those ingredients to prepare meals for partner organizations. Unused items go to the agencies too.

"We have always had enough food around," Kamar said. "But now what we are seeing is every day the shelves are empty at the end of the day, so every bit of food that comes into our kitchen every day goes right back out to the community at the end of the day."

The decrease in Snap enrollment has also affected schools' ability to provide free meals to students. If at least 25% of a student body are recipients of Snap or some other public benefits, the school can participate in the Community Eligibility Provision (Cep) program and use federal funds to provide free breakfast and lunch to all students without needing household applications.

But because fewer students are enrolled in Snap, that has made it harder for schools to serve those free meals to students who need them, the Washington Post reported this week. In Houston independent school district, 26 schools that previously provided free meals to all students under Cep are no longer eligible for the program, according to the Post.

Anti-hunger advocates also say that the employment data does not support the argument that more people have found jobs or seen their wages increase and thus no longer need food stamps. The United States added 776,000 non-farm jobs between January 2025 and September 2026. During the last 20 months of Joe Biden's presidency, the country added 2.6 million non-farm jobs, according to Factcheck.org .

"We don't have the data to suggest that there are more jobs suddenly out there. We just know fewer people are getting benefits," said Sheril Kirshenbaum, Food Bank Council of Michigan's chief external relations officer.

A USDA spokesperson downplayed the effect of the Snap restrictions.

"The number of individuals receiving benefits is constantly changing and is not representative of any one policy," the spokesperson stated in an email to the Guardian.

It could soon become even harder for people struggling with food insecurity. States will now have to pay for most of the Snap administrative costs while also preparing for an October 2027 change that will require states to pay for some of Snap benefit costs if their payment error rate is above 6%, which according to the USDA, is not a measure of fraud . (Paradoxically, states that had error rates above 13% received a delay in implementation of the requirement.)

States will now be having to pay more for existing work while also finding funding for extra work to reduce the error rate, said Joseph Llobrera, senior director of research for the food assistance team at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

That could mean longer processing times and people who need assistance having to wait longer to get it, Kirshenbaum said.

"States have been really set up to fail," Llobrera said.

The USDA spokesperson did not respond to a question about concerns that the Snap changes have forced some Americans to go hungry.

A Louisville woman, Sandra Scott, 58, has been homeless most of her life and said that until she started receiving Snap benefits four years ago, she ate at "soup kitchens or wherever I could, but for the most part, like on the weekends, there really was not anywhere to go".

Scott has had six back surgeries and struggled with mental illness. She became addicted to methamphetamines but got sober two years ago and now lives in a subsidized apartment. She is working to obtain her emergency responder certificate and volunteers with The Table, a non-profit restaurant that uses a pay-what-you-can model.

Asked what she would say to members of the Trump administration about the Snap changes, Scott said: "Why don't you walk in one of our shoes, somebody in the community that doesn't have anything, that wasn't born into money or doesn't have a job because it's so hard to find or [who] can't find affordable housing because it's too high?"

articles.title: 'Some still allow political calculations': Jaishankar's veiled swipe days after Rubio backs Pak ties
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said that the use of terrorism as an “instrument of statecraft” was unacceptable and could
articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said that the use of terrorism as an “instrument of statecraft” was unacceptable and could never be justified, warning that the threat persisted because some countries did not demonstrate “zero tolerance”.Speaking at the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan on the occasion of UN Day, Jaishankar said some countries continued to allow political considerations to take precedence despite the lessons of history.“Terrorism is another deadly threat to peace. Its usage as an instrument of statecraft is simply unacceptable. It can never be justified. It can never be rationalised. Yet, it continues because not all states really display zero tolerance,” he said.“Despite history holding so many lessons, some still allow political calculations to take precedence. The world must therefore develop sharper awareness about this common threat, and it must come together with stronger resolve and counter-terrorism in all its forms and manifestations,” he added. Jaishankar did not name any country in his remarks.Earlier this week, US secretary of state Marco Rubio defended Washington’s engagement with Pakistan saying the US needed to maintain relations with countries with which it had disagreements.Speaking to Network18, Rubio said Pakistan’s possession of nuclear weapons and its geographical position made engagement necessary.He also argued that maintaining ties could give Washington greater influence over Islamabad’s decisions, including on terrorism.“In the case of Pakistan, it’s a country that we have to have a relationship with, a country that possesses nuclear weapons. It’s a country that from a geographic standpoint, we need to be able to interact with them in much the same way as govt of India has to have and has a relationship and meets with leaders from Iran,” Rubio said.“... It could be a positive thing because if... we can speak to them, it perhaps puts us in a position to help discourage the kinds of things India is worried about,” he added.Rubio also urged businesses to view India-US ties as a strategic partnership spanning technology, trade and security. He said the two countries were “perfectly aligned” on issues shaping the 21st century, while acknowledging that differences would persist.Jaishankar also stressed the importance of peace amid ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia, warning that wars in one part of the world can have far-reaching consequences for global security, economies and societies."We cannot remain helpless spectators. India expresses global sentiment when we urge that dialogue and diplomacy are the only solution," the external affairs minister said.Emphasising the interconnected nature of global peace, he said, "Let us consider the indivisibility of peace. Now, war anywhere threatens peace everywhere."Jaishankar said India was making efforts towards peacebuilding and remained open to working with other partners to advance these efforts.The minister also highlighted the link between peace, economic progress and shared prosperity, warning that unequal development in an interconnected world could fuel further instability."Progress and prosperity are the flip side of conflict and violence, and they too are equally indivisible. The world cannot advance half prosperous and half denied in an era of intricate supply chains, of globalised markets, and of common resources. This is simply a prescription for continuous instability," he said.His remarks came a day after India condemned a deadly attack on a church in Karak, Jordan, on October 23, which killed seven people and injured 34 others.In a statement, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) described the attack as “heinous” and “cowardly”, extended condolences to the bereaved families and wished those injured a speedy recovery.Jaishankar also called for reforms in the United Nations, saying the organisation's shortcomings and limitations needed to be acknowledged and addressed. He said the case for reformed multilateralism was becoming increasingly compelling."Large parts of the world cannot be left out from decision-making. The UN must show leadership, not be a spectator to global crises," he said.Calling for collective efforts to strengthen the international body, he added, "On this occasion, even as we recognise the need for such long-awaited changes, let us renew our commitment to work together. We are common, we are shared, we are united."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?
articles.summary: Reports say Pentagon has drawn up plans for strikes after midterm polls, but analysts question what it could achieve.
articles.body:
The US military has drawn up options for renewed attacks on Iran, according to the Washington-based website The Hill, raising the prospect of another round of major fighting in a war approaching its eighth month.

Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US forces in the Middle East, has plans ready for follow-up strikes if authorised by the White House, the outlet reported. It also said military planners had prepared several options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The report focused on possible attacks after the November 3 US midterm elections. But President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that the United States could strike as soon as “tomorrow”, while also holding out the possibility of a “big, beautiful” agreement with Tehran.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, accused Washington of derailing negotiations but said efforts to reach an agreement should continue. With both sides warning of further attacks, could the conflict tip back into full-scale war? Here is what we know.

The latest reporting suggests military preparations are advancing, although it remains unclear which options Trump might approve or when. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the Pentagon had instructed CENTCOM to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations. Its sources said a renewed campaign could target Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear sites.

Those preparations do not amount to an order to attack. The decision ultimately rests with Trump, whose public statements continue to leave room for both military action and negotiations.

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have drawn up joint plans for an attack on Iran after the midterm elections. The reports come alongside US warnings about alleged Iranian threats to American personnel overseas. An intelligence memo sent on Friday by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel”, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and elsewhere.

The Department of State has ordered staffing reductions at several regional embassies amid the warnings. The publicly reported memo did not identify specific targets or establish when any alleged attacks might occur.

Trump has added to the uncertainty. At a rally on Friday, he said Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the codename of the US-Israeli military operation against Iran that began on February 28. On Saturday, he declined to disclose the timing of any possible attack while suggesting one could come as early as Sunday.

Julie Norman, associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera the preparations served both as short-term posturing and a possible longer-term military objective next month. “With Trump, I think he is always keeping options on the table, but I think this particular drawing up of plans is an immediate posturing deterrent, but also a very real option after the midterms,” she said.

It comes as the US is deploying a third aircraft carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with roughly 10,000 additional soldiers and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East by the end of November.

Tehran has combined calls for further negotiations with warnings that renewed US attacks would bring a wider response. “We were having negotiations, the cowards [Americans] messed everything up,” Pezeshkian said in remarks broadcast on Saturday, before adding that efforts to conclude the agreement should continue.

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf will also miss the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi, according to the Iranian Embassy in India. The embassy cited “unforeseen circumstances” without elaborating.

On Sunday, Iran’s army also said it had shot down a US-developed LUCAS drone over the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

The Reuters news agency has reported, quoting Iranian security officials, that Tehran has drawn up plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of a resumption of US and Israeli attacks.

The incident followed Iranian claims that seven oil tankers had caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week, while on Wednesday, Iran also announced what it describes as a shift towards an “offensive” military doctrine, warning that countries hosting bases used in US attacks could become targets.

“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.

The warning raises the prospect of a confrontation spreading further across the region, with energy infrastructure and countries aligned with Washington potentially exposed. “Iran is also drawing up its own target lists to include energy infrastructure and US-aligned states,” Norman said.

“So I would say both parties are certainly very prepared for another round of escalation and projecting preparedness to each other.”

“In the meantime, there is a very high risk of miscalculation by either side, a very high risk of rapid escalation.”

October has become the worst month for attacks on ships since the war began in February, with more than 120 attacks reported so far.

Would another attack serve Trump’s interests?

The timing is politically sensitive, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing for an attack as his support dwindles in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s election.

It comes after Netanyahu said overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”.

Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies in Qatar, said recent developments pointed towards renewed fighting rather than a diplomatic breakthrough. “There is a lot of signalling, a lot of posturing suggesting that we are headed for another round of fighting,” he told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to Hegseth’s recent visit to Israel, and Washington’s reported withdrawal of personnel from regional diplomatic and military sites. “All of that would suggest that the US and Israel are planning [another round of attacks] on Iran, either soon or very soon,” he said.

“One of the fears is this next round of fighting could actually be more dangerous, more catastrophic than the previous round.”

Norman added that while the US president may be eyeing up a strike on Iran after the midterms, “the big question for Trump from military advisers is – what would a further round of escalation bring that the other rounds didn’t?”

“What would these strategies do to force Iran to the negotiating table? And I don’t think there has been a clear answer to that.”

articles.title: Project aims to boost AI across tourism sector in South West
articles.summary: The University of Plymouth says students and graduates will work with the tourism sector.
articles.body:
A project has been launched to help the tourism industry benefit from advances in artificial intelligence (AI).

The University of Plymouth said the £275,000 project would allow students and graduates to work with people in tourism on a "range of exciting initiatives".

Rong Huang, programme lead in tourism and hospitality at Plymouth Business School, said: "This project brings our students, our industry partners and regional employers together so that learning happens on live business challenges."

Claire Steiner, from the Institute of Travel and Tourism, added: "AI is changing how we work in travel and tourism, and we need to make sure people have the skills and confidence to use it well."

Steiner said the project would bring employers' views and experience into what was taught at the university to help create practical learning opportunities.

"We'll also share what we learn across the UK, helping both current and future tourism professionals use AI responsibly and effectively," she said.

The university said the South West Visitor Economy AI Skills Accelerator was part of a collaboration between the university, the Institute of Travel and Tourism, Destination Plymouth, Women in Travel CIC, Building Brands and Brand Biscuit.

The university asked any tourism, hospitality and marketing businesses interested in hosting a traineeship or internship, or proposing an AI challenge, to get in contact.

It said graduates and working professionals interested in developing their AI skills were invited to register their interest with the university.

Dave Briggs, founder of Building Brands, said: "For us, it's about making AI more accessible, practical and genuinely valuable to businesses across the South West."

articles.title: More questions than answers: Arch Manning likes the disrespect, Big 12's disaster and a CFP race in disarray
articles.summary: No. 2 BYU fell to UCF in double overtime after chaos erupted in regulation, while Texas Tech lost to unranked Cincinnati in a wild Big 12 weekend.
articles.body: So, turns out 'survival weekend' in college football did not go as planned for a number of teams across the country on Saturday, as for the consecutive weeks the No. 2 ranked team in the sport went down in dramatic fashion. This time it was No. 2 BYU falling victim to the hangover, losing to UCF in double-overtime that turned into pure chaos over the final few minutes of regulation, after defeating Notre Dame last week. And, maybe Steve Sarkisian was right this past week in the buildup to the Ole Miss showdown that everyone involved in the talk around Arch Manning, even if warranted, created a monster in the Texas quarterback. How did Arch feel about the commentary around him this week? He admitted it's a never ending cycle, though he's starting to enjoy the doubters in his 'edgy' era. "I've been hyped up all my life, the preseason and all this stuff," Manning explained after the win over Ole Miss. "I think I kida like being disregarded kinda now." ARCH MANNING, TEXAS SURVIVE OLE MISS AFTER ANOTHER SECOND HALF MELTDOWN CREATES ANXIETY IN AUSTIN AFTER REBELS FRENZY COMEBACK A win over the No. 7 Rebels have put the Longhorns back into the CFP conversation in dramatic fashion, with a statement win over an Ole Miss team who was coming off a bye-week. It was also the Big 12 Conference that was at the forefront of madness this week, taking a page out of the SEC's playbook after last weekend, while both No. 15 Iowa and No. 16 USC lost in Big Ten play. Did we expect Texas Tech to go on the road and lose to unranked Cincinnati? No, but we also didn’t think the Red Raiders would look so lethargic in the process behind their expensive roster that is partially funded by mega-booster Cody Campbell. The fact is that there is so much parity across college football right now that nothing should come as a surprise any longer, at least not during the 2026 season. Whether it's Oregon losing its third game of the year, with a disaster of a performance against Illinois, or Michigan taking Indiana to overtime in the 'Big House', there is a weird vibe around the sport currently. Who in the world are the best teams in college football? Arch Manning helps Texas upset No. 7 Ole Miss, South Carolina stuns No. 11 Tennessee What in the world is in the water around the Texas football facility? One minute it's Arch Manning putting on a show for college football fans, and then it's the Longhorns going cold in the second half that has us all wondering why there is this tale of two halves with this Steve Sarkisian offense. What we witnessed on Saturday night in Austin was essentially just another night in the SEC. A back-and-forth slugfest between two teams that are capable of making a college football playoff run if everything is clicking. Somebody had to lose, and we still have plenty of questions lingering around both teams coming out of this one. DID WE CREATE A MONSTER? ARCH MANNING'S 'AW SHUCKS' PERSONA IS GONE Trinidad Chambliss is still that dude, as he proved in the second half of this matchup, and Arch Manning is still trying to figure out how to play consistent football for four quarters. Each team is still in the running for the SEC title game, while every conference team besides Georgia and Kentucky has two losses. And yes, that list now includes Tennessee after a fourth quarter frenzy by South Carolina. I think Tennessee fans are still trying to figure out how they lost that football game, or putting some of the blame on the officiating (which i'd understand). But, when the Vols couldn’t get out of their own way, South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers and defensive end Dylan Stewart kicked the door down. Another one of those hangovers, right? Maybe, but after a dominating performance against Alabama last week, one would’ve expected a better outing from the No. 11 ranked team in the country during the most important times of the game. articles.title: AI in policing risks deepening discrimination, research warns
articles.summary: AI tools learn from biased records and may deepen discrimination against minorities without oversight, researchers say.
articles.body:
In his award-winning essay, young British science writer Adrian Dredge wrote about the potential pitfalls of AI and policing.

The essay won the 2026 Young Science Writer Award , chosen each year by the Association of British Science Writers. Here is an edited version of the entry.

The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.

Studies suggest that predictions of future crime hotspots may be based on biased data, which can magnify existing prejudice and create a dangerous feedback loop.

Experts are calling for the use of AI in policing to be reviewed with greater human oversight.

This would involve checking the data that forces use to find and remove any bias, according to Dr Carolyn McKay, an associate professor and researcher in digital justice at the University of Sydney Law School.

"The public functions of state policing ought to be subject to human oversight and scrutiny," she says.

The problem, according to McKay, is that AI systems are trained on data that already contains human bias, and this can lead to self-fulfilling prophecies.

Think of AI as a map-maker asked to draw a map of a city they have never visited. They are locked in a windowless room and can't go outside. All they have are maps that are 50 years old.

Anyone following the new map would find themselves stopping at walls that were knocked down years ago and looking for roads that no longer exist. The map-maker hasn't made anything new. They have only copied the old maps.

Now suppose the map-maker is handed a list of past crimes and where they took place, and asked to shade in where the next ones are likely to happen. Police then patrol the shaded areas.

More crime is recorded there simply because more officers are there to see it. Areas outside the shading appear to have less crime, because fewer people are looking. When the next map is drawn, the same areas are shaded even darker.

So the crime figures are not a full list of crimes. They are partly a record of where police have chosen to look.

The problem is as old as policing, but AI may be speeding it up.

Sarah Brayne, a sociologist at the University of Texas at Austin, spent time inside the Los Angeles Police Department studying how it uses big data. In her research paper, published in the American Sociological Review, she found that the force increasingly used data to predict crime, rather than only to respond to it.

She also found that the data fed into these systems was skewed. Crimes in public places were more likely to be seen and recorded, and police focus was disproportionately on black neighbourhoods. Once this goes into the system, she writes, "the predictions appear impartial".

The models, she says, create "a feedback loop in which they not only predict events such as crime or police contact, but also contribute to their future occurrence."

But that is a view challenged by Dr Dimitrios Kollias, an associate professor in multimodal artificial intelligence at the Queen Mary University of London (QMUL). He says that the technology has moved on to take the bias of historical data into account.

"The old-map analogy is useful for explaining how historical bias can be inherited, but it has its limits," he told BBC News.

"Modern AI systems do not simply retrieve or copy their training examples; they can combine learned information in new ways and generate outputs and solutions that were not explicitly present in those examples."

But those new insights pose a separate risk, Kollias adds.

"As AI systems become more capable of generating novel decisions and acting with greater autonomy, we need to ensure that their behaviour remains safe, reliable and under meaningful human control," he said.

But arguably a more intractable problem is dealing with the sometimes flawed information stored by authorities and which AI systems draw from.

Researchers at New York University said that many of their predictions may rely on what they call "dirty data". These are police records shaped, they say, by corrupt, biased or unlawful practices, including rigged crime figures and arrests of innocent people.

In their study, the researchers found that in nine of the 13 US areas they looked at, police data from periods of unlawful or biased policing was available to train these systems.

The system can't tell that this data is flawed, according to the researchers. It simply treats it as a pattern to repeat. It is as if the map-maker's compass points only to where crime has been recorded before. The map-maker thinks they have found a new crime hotspot, when all they have done is follow the bias of earlier officers.

McKay's answer is to have someone independent check the map before anyone uses it and rub out the lines that are wrong.

But cleaning up dirty data won't be easy. The mistakes aren't a few stray pencil marks. The whole map has been drawn on top of them. The New York University researchers say that technical fixes offered by the companies selling these systems aren't enough unless someone independently checks how the data was produced in the first place.

Because AI can see the world only through the data it is given, it can make serious mistakes which can harm people.

For example, a 2019 study in the journal Science looked at an AI system used in US healthcare to help decide which patients should get extra support. It did this by predicting whose care would cost the most. But there was an inherent bias in the data it drew from. Less was already being spent on black patients than on equally ill white patients, partly because of poorer access to care. By treating higher costs as a sign of greater need, the system unfairly favoured white patients.

It was as if the map-maker had been told to mark the sickest parts of the city but had marked the places where the most money was spent instead. When the researchers changed the system to predict how ill patients were, rather than how much their care would cost, the bias largely disappeared. The share of black patients picked for extra help would have risen from about 18% to 47%.

Kollias acknowledges that AI bias from dirty data is "an important concern".

"But this does not mean that bias is inevitable." he says.

"We can test systems for unfair outcomes, improve the data and objectives they use, and introduce safeguards to reduce these effects."

One improvement would be to provide additional data that provides context. What if the map-maker were given more than a list of crimes? They could also be shown which areas have been neglected - places with broken streetlights, little funding and missing public services. That could show whether the local environment plays a part. Instead of sending police cars to the shaded areas, councils might send money to fix the lighting, support the community and repair the area itself.

Yet even this may not be enough, according to McKay.

"The target environments are still intimately linked with their inhabitants," she says. "They might (continue to) be over-policed and marginalised."

She points to systems which were designed to use information about places rather than people. Even so, critics raised concerns that they still led to over-policing.

Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened

It is as if the map-maker promised to stop writing people's names on the map and to mark only the streets and buildings. But those streets were shaded because of years of neglect and heavy policing, so rubbing out the names changes very little.

AI has no beliefs or personality of its own. Like the map-maker in the windowless room, it knows only what it is told. If the person describing the city holds a grudge against one neighbourhood, that grudge ends up on the map.

But ultimately the problem is the human bias that fed the AI. People decide what a suspicious person looks like on CCTV, or what counts as a risky loan, and they bring their own cultural, educational and political biases with them. So perhaps AI can be part of the solution rather than a magnifier of the problem, says Kollias.

"A carefully designed and independently evaluated AI system can make some of these patterns more measurable and visible, giving us an opportunity to identify and reduce them."

But humans too have to play their part. The healthcare study shows that those choices can be checked and changed. That is why researchers argue that people must stay in the loop. Otherwise, like a map-maker inking over old pencil lines, AI risks leaving us all in a windowless room, permanently trapped in yesterday's mistakes.

articles.title: Algerian parliament’s upper house approves troop deployment to Niger
articles.summary: Vote to send forces comes after a recent defence pact between the two neighbouring countries.
articles.body:
The upper house of Algeria’s parliament has unanimously approved the deployment of troops to neighbouring Niger.

The Algerian constitution empowers the president to send military units abroad, provided that both chambers of parliament approve it by a two-thirds majority.

The Council of the Nation held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on troop deployment, while the People’s National Assembly, or the lower house, is expected to hold a separate session later in the evening, Algeria’s popular newspaper El Khabar reported. If the deployment is approved, it would be the first mission outside Algeria’s borders since the 1973 War between Israel and several Arab countries, known to Arabs as the October War and Israelis as the Yom Kippur War.

The military units to be deployed by Algeria are expected to be tasked with securing oil facilities in Niger.

The vote came after a visit by Niger’s Defence Minister General Salifou Modi to Algeria last week, where he held talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Chief of Staff of the People’s National Army General Said Chanegriha.

During that visit, the two sides signed a military cooperation protocol, the details of which were not made public.

Earlier this month, Tebboune confirmed that Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger in late August to help thwart a “ coup attempt ” that shook the capital, Niamey.

The Algerian Ministry of Defence previously said it had sent four jets to Niger following the unrest. It said two patrols of four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft had landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an air-to-air refuelling plane.

The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilise the brotherly state of Niger”, the ministry said on August 30.

Relations between Algeria and Niger have witnessed a significant rapprochement over the past few months on political, diplomatic, military and economic levels, following a period of tension between the two countries.

articles.title: Bill Ackman urges Israelis to exclude far-right ministers ahead of elections
articles.summary: Billionaire hedge fund investor Bill Ackman called for Israel’s next government to exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich days before Israeli voters head to the polls, arguing that both have damaged the country’s international reputation. “Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements…
articles.body:
Billionaire hedge fund investor Bill Ackman called for Israel’s next government to exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich days before Israeli voters head to the polls, arguing that both have damaged the country’s international reputation.

“Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions which are presented in the global media as representing the voice and will of all Israelis,” Ackman wrote in a post on the social platform X .

Ackman, a prominent supporter of Israel, said he was adding his perspective as “someone who has an understanding of how Israel is perceived in America,” saying their controversial positions are often portrayed internationally as reflecting the views of Israelis more broadly.

“As such, a government formed without Ben-Gvir and Smotrich will send a message to the rest of the world that Israel is turning a new page,” he continued. “This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large.”

Ackman stopped short of endorsing a candidate for prime minister, saying the choice should be left to Israeli citizens.

His comments come two days before Israel’s election on Oct. 27, in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking another term against a field of challengers led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the centrist Yashar party.

Recent polls have shown Eisenkot’s party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud, though neither side has a clear path to securing the 61 seats needed to form a government in Israel’s 120-member parliament, nor has a single party ever won a majority in the parliament.

Netanyahu has emphasized his close relationship with President Trump, who endorsed him, and the threat posed by Iran. Ben-Gvir, who leads the ultranationalist Otzma Yehudit party, and Smotrich, who leads the Religious Zionism party, have both drawn international criticism over their extremist views on Palestinians and Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Bulgaria holds a presidential election dominated by economic hardship and the Ukraine war
articles.summary: Bulgarians headed to the polls on Sunday to elect their next president in a campaign centered on growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping.
articles.body: Bulgarians headed to the polls on Sunday to elect their next president in a campaign centered on growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The vote will also be the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev after its triumph in parliamentary elections in April. Despite a record number of candidates, the race is expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, backed by Radev’s party, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties. The campaign has focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country. The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict and prompted the government to ask Bulgaria’s partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security. Candidates have also sought to address public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet. Polling stations, which opened at 7 a.m., are to close at 8 p.m., after which initial exit polls will be announced while preliminary results are expected on Monday. The election will likely go into a runoff as none of the 27 candidates is expected to win outright. Turnout must be above 50% of 6.6 million registered voters, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Projections have Sunday’s turnout at less than 40%, indicating a likely Nov. 1 runoff. Yotova, a 62-year-old journalist and former member of the European Parliament, is the country’s incumbent president and a front-runner in the race. She previously served as vice president under Radev, during his two terms as head of state. She took over the presidency in January 2026, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now seeking her own mandate. She’s running as an independent but also has the official backing of Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party, where her career began. If she wins, Yotova will become Bulgaria’s first elected female president. Analysts expect her to continue Radev’s policy to keep Bulgaria on its European path but at the same time call for improved relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine. Addressing supporters at a rally this week, Yotova said she “advocated for peace through negotiations, rather than force”. Observers say that Yotova’s victory would keep the presidency in the hands of the ruling majority, and such concentration of power could prevent institutions maintaining effective checks and balances on policy decisions. Yotova’s main challenger is economist Andrei Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister who led the country in the early months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition. Gyurov, who has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership. “I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position,” he told supporters this week. Latest opinion polls give Yotova an edge in the first round of the race by giving her between 40 percent and 45 percent, versus Gyurov’s 25-30 %, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. But some observers believe that Gyurov could have a better chance in a runoff, where results can be influenced by voters who supported candidates eliminated in the first round. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. While the post is primarily ceremonial, the direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

articles.title: Musk accuses Ukraine of violating Starlink’s terms of service following dispute over coverage
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Ukraine’s military of violating Starlink’s terms of service, after Kyiv said that access to the service had been restored.
articles.body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Ukraine’s military of violating Starlink’s terms of service, after Kyiv said that access to the service had been restored. In a post on X Saturday, Musk said that Ukraine’s armed forces had “violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” “That loophole was closed last week,” he added, referring to the restrictions temporarily placed on the service last week which limited speeds to 100 miles per hour. Musk also maintained that Starshield is a separate system controlled by the US government. Musk also underscored Ukraine’s reliance on the service, saying it “remains critical to the defense of Ukraine” and claimed that if Starlink were turned off, “the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately.” Zelensky’s adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov disputed Musk’s accusation that Ukraine is using the commercial service to kill people, saying speed restrictions and the service’s unavailability over Russian territory made Ukraine “physically unable to use commercial Starlink” for medium- and long-range strikes into Russia. Serhiy Sternenko, a former Ukrainian Ministry of Defense adviser, also denied Musk’s claims. “As someone who was involved in the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko said. Echoing Beskrestnov’s claims, he said, “It was technically impossible to use the civilian Starlink system for drone missions. All drone missions requiring satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.” Ukraine’s defense ministry said Saturday that full access to Starlink and Starshield was restored. It came after US President Donald Trump said he asked Musk to lift restrictions on Kyiv’s use of the military grade version of the Musk-owned Starlink internet service. “The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording a recovery in Starlink/Starshield speeds,” Ukrainian Minister of Defense Yevheniy Khmara said in a statement, adding that restored speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour were being recorded. For more than a week, Ukraine had faced a speed limit on the Starshield satellite terminals used by its military, hindering its ability to intercept fast-moving Russian drones. Trump and his top officials have denied making the call to throttle Ukraine’s use of Starshield, which limited speeds to 100 mph, according to Ukrainian officials. Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a post to social media last week. It comes as Russia’s attacks on Ukraine continued overnight. According to Ukrainian authorities, over 153 Russian Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) were launched at Ukraine from Russia, mainly targeting large department stores and warehouses. At least three people were killed in the UAV strikes and 25 others were injured. Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said at least two were killed and 22 injured in Ukrainian attacks. 532 UAVs fired from Ukraine were intercepted, the MoD said, adding that industrial sites were hit in multiple regions.

articles.title: Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
articles.summary: Children in Gaza with auditory and visual challenges often have no access to specialist education.
articles.body:
Gaza City – With the help of his father, 13-year-old Kenan al-Sabaa attempts to adjust his hearing aid, which has malfunctioned. The plastic tubing and rubber ear mould on the device need fixing, but these parts and the depleted batteries are no longer available due to Israel’s siege on the Gaza Strip.

Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started in October 2023, Kenan attended the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, which provided specialist teaching and opportunities to communicate with other hearing-impaired children.

But Atfaluna’s building in Gaza City was partially levelled during the war and quickly turned into an overcrowded shelter for displaced people, an example of the widespread destruction of infrastructure in Gaza. This includes the educational institutions disabled children rely upon.

Israeli attacks also forced Kenan’s family to flee to Gaza City’s Jalaa Street. Atfaluna has since set up temporary learning spaces, and Kenan has access to one near where his family now lives. But his father, Tamer al-Sabaa, said the interruptions to his learning during the war have left his son far behind in his studies.

He did not attend school at all during the first year of the war, and now attends classes only for a few hours a week, which Tamer says is not enough given the time he has lost at school during the war.

But Tamer fears that if Israel resumes large-scale attacks – an October 2025 “ceasefire” reduced the number of attacks but did not stop them – he will be forced to stop Kenan from attending.

“These few hours do not cover or repair the massive educational gap and academic decline my son experienced during the war,” Tamer said. “He is in dire need of restoring his equipped educational environment and the specialised care that was stripped away from him.”

“The school operates only three days a week, and for limited hours not exceeding two hours a day,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Being deaf makes Kenan’s movements fraught with danger, as he cannot hear the sounds of explosions, warning signals, or communicate with those around him.”

As a result, Tamer and his wife had to guide Kenan through unfamiliar neighbourhoods to help him learn about his surroundings.

Kenan can now reach school independently, but his safety is always a concern for his parents.

The difficulties facing Kenan highlight the effect of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, on disabled children in the enclave.

Fadel Kuraz, a sign language interpreter and disability rights advocate with Atfaluna, said the war has increased hearing-related injuries and severely weakened the services available to children who need support.

“What we are experiencing today in the Gaza Strip represents an unprecedented health and humanitarian setback, and a real catastrophe unlike anything we have seen before,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.

“To grasp the scale of the tragedy, the baseline number of persons with hearing disabilities registered before October 2023 was around 20,000 people. Today, according to field assessments, approximately 35,000 new individuals … have been added, having suffered total or partial hearing loss due to … explosions.”

Kuraz describes shortages of hearing aids, batteries, ear moulds, and spare parts, alongside major obstacles to specialist hearing tests and treatments. Children also face difficulties accessing visual learning materials because of electricity and communications outages, he said.

“The suffering does not stop at material needs. A deaf child suffers high levels of fear, stress and complex trauma without the ability to verbally express what is on their mind,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.

Hearing-impaired children in Gaza are more often than not living in overcrowded tents or shelters which lack privacy or a proper space to do homework and study.

“I emphasise that responding to the needs of persons with hearing disabilities is no longer a secondary choice or a luxury; it is an urgent humanitarian necessity,” Kuraz adds. “It requires immediate intervention to break the siege, allow the entry of hearing aids, batteries, and spare parts, and establish safe, temporary alternative educational spaces to replace destroyed centres.”

Children with visual impairments face issues similar to those faced by hearing-impaired children in Gaza, with the few educational facilities once available to them now closed or difficult to access. The materials and items they need to study, such as Braille, are also difficult to procure due to Israel’s siege on Gaza.

Al-Noor school was originally located in Tal al-Hawa, southwest of Gaza City, but was badly damaged in the genocidal war.

Duaa Omar Basheer worked as an educational counsellor at the al-Noor school for blind students in northern Gaza before the war. She said it was the only public school in Gaza designated for middle and high school students with visual impairments, but was forced to close during the war. Some primary education is available to children through educational centres run by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

Previously, the school served about 80 pupils from across Gaza, many of whom arrived on dedicated buses, but damaged roads and a lack of suitable transport created further barriers.

Without regular instruction, Basheer fears students could lose their Braille and independent-learning skills, which they have taken years to learn.

“We are facing an entire generation of visually-impaired individuals at risk of illiteracy and academic loss,” Basheer said.

In the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City, Jana Shreim’s mother, Wafaa Shreim, says her 12-year-old daughter, who is legally blind, relies on prescription glasses with high magnification and very strong lenses. But she could still only perceive light, shapes and nearby objects.

Her glasses broke amid the harrowing mass exodus from the Shati camp during Israel’s offensive on the neighbourhood in November 2023. The family tried to fix them with wire, but the lenses were damaged beyond use, and replacement glasses were too expensive.

Since the glasses broke – and with no possibility of replacing them due to the blockade – her vision has deteriorated to the point that she can barely see.

Now, when Jana goes to unfamiliar places, she stumbles and falls. Her mother says she is bullied by other children, and that she experiences pain in her eyes when she tries to focus.

“My daughter now has to identify people by their voices,” Wafaa told Al Jazeera. “Her sister and I now act as her ‘eyes’ at every step and everywhere she goes.”

Before the war, Jana attended the al-Noor centre, travelling there on a dedicated bus service. Her school closed when it was badly damaged in Israeli bombing, leaving Jana without any access to education.

“I am currently trying to teach her at home myself using a Braille writing machine we have, so she doesn’t lose her limited educational skills,” Jana’s mother said. She also cares for another daughter with a visual impairment, making it even more difficult to provide the specialist support they both need.

“I searched extensively and knocked on the doors of many institutions and organisations concerned with visual impairment, but the bitter truth is that … we have been left entirely alone,” she said.

“My only message and wish to all responsible parties is to look at our visually impaired children with mercy: provide them with glasses and medical supplies, and open safe educational and recreational spaces that restore their basic right to life and learning.”

articles.title: In 2023, Damar Hamlin survived cardiac arrest during an NFL game; three years later, he helped a Pittsburgh event set a CPR training record with 1,293 people completing training in one hour
articles.summary: NFL safety Damar Hamlin has helped 1,293 people learn hands-only CPR in just one hour in Pittsburgh, setting a Guinness World Record and bringing his
articles.body: NFL safety Damar Hamlin has helped 1,293 people learn hands-only CPR in just one hour in Pittsburgh, setting a Guinness World Record and bringing his campaign to improve emergency response training to his home city. The event was held at Acrisure Stadium during the NFL Draft, in partnership with the American Heart Association, the National Football League and Dr Mikhail Varshavski, widely known online as Dr Mike. The group aimed to teach as many people as possible how to respond when someone suffers a cardiac arrest. The 60-minute session broke the previous record for the most people taught hands-only CPR at one location within an hour. Participants received practical instruction and practised chest compressions on training manikins under the supervision of certified instructors and Guinness World Records adjudicators. The achievement carries particular meaning for Hamlin, who survived a cardiac arrest during a Buffalo Bills game in January 2023. Medical staff performed CPR on the pitch, helping save his life. Since then, he has worked to raise awareness of CPR, access to defibrillators and the need for people to act quickly during medical emergencies.Hamlin's experience drives CPR campaignHamlin, a native of McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, played college football at the University of Pittsburgh before joining the Buffalo Bills in the NFL. Returning to his home city for the record attempt gave him an opportunity to support a cause closely linked to his own experience. Speaking about the gathering, Hamlin said: "To see so many people come together in my hometown to learn this life-saving skill is deeply moving. Knowing that nearly 1,300 more people now have the confidence to step up in an emergency is incredible. This is about giving families more time together, just like I was given." His cardiac arrest took place during a Monday Night Football game against the Cincinnati Bengals on 2 January 2023. The incident led to widespread concern as medical staff treated him on the pitch before he was taken to hospital. Hamlin later returned to professional football and became an advocate for CPR education and wider access to automated external defibrillators (AEDs). His recovery has also helped bring greater attention to the role that immediate action can play when someone's heart suddenly stops. According to the American Heart Association, CPR can double or triple a person's chances of surviving an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest when it is started promptly.Why hands-only CPR mattersHands-only CPR is a simplified form of cardiopulmonary resuscitation that focuses on chest compressions. It is designed to help members of the public respond quickly when an adult suddenly collapses and is unresponsive and not breathing normally. The American Heart Association recommends pushing hard and fast in the centre of the chest, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. People should call emergency services and ask someone to find an AED if one is available. Unlike conventional CPR, hands-only CPR does not require mouth-to-mouth rescue breaths. This can make it easier for people without formal medical training to act while waiting for emergency responders. At the Pittsburgh event, participants practised the technique on training manikins as instructors guided them through the process. Guinness World Records adjudicators monitored the session to confirm that the record requirements were met. Dr Mike, who took part in the initiative alongside Hamlin, stressed the need for people to recognise a cardiac emergency and respond without delay. "Cardiac arrest can happen to anyone, anywhere, at any time. The difference between life and death often comes down to whether someone nearby knows what to do and acts quickly." The American Heart Association says more than 350,000 cardiac arrests occur outside hospitals in the United States each year. Many happen in homes or other places where a family member, friend or member of the public may be the first person able to help.A national effort to improve survivalThe Pittsburgh record attempt formed part of the American Heart Association's wider Nation of Lifesavers campaign, which aims to double survival rates from sudden cardiac arrest by 2030. The association has called for more people to learn CPR, pointing to the gap between the number of people who suffer cardiac arrest outside hospitals and those who receive help before emergency services arrive. Its published figures show that survival remains low. The association's 2025 CPR guidance reports that around 350,000 people experience an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest annually in the US, with roughly 10 per cent surviving. Immediate CPR can improve the chances of survival while medical teams prepare further treatment. The record-setting session at Acrisure Stadium was intended to give hundreds of families and community members practical skills they could use in an emergency. Rather than limiting training to healthcare workers, the initiative encouraged ordinary members of the public to learn the basics.Expanding access to defibrillatorsHamlin has also supported efforts to make emergency equipment more widely available through his charitable organisation, The Chasing M's Foundation. The foundation has worked to distribute AEDs and support educational programmes involving schools, youth sports leagues and community organisations. AEDs can analyse a person's heart rhythm and deliver an electric shock when needed to help restore a normal rhythm. The NFL has also backed wider emergency preparedness measures, including emergency action plans and access to life-saving equipment at sports and recreational facilities. The American Heart Association and the league worked with Hamlin and Dr Mike to organise the Pittsburgh training session. According to the association's announcement on 27 April 2026, the 1,293 participants completed hands-only CPR training in one hour during the second day of the NFL Draft on 24 April. For Hamlin, the achievement linked a personal experience with a public health effort. articles.title: US midterms 2026: Indian-born Nithya Raman challenges LA mayor Karen Bass
articles.summary: Nithya Raman, an urban planner and Los Angeles City Council member born in India, is challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in the November 3, 2026,
articles.body: Nithya Raman, an urban planner and Los Angeles City Council member born in India, is challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in the November 3, 2026, election, promising to tackle the city's housing crisis, homelessness and deteriorating public services. Although the contest is taking place alongside the US midterms, it is a municipal election, not a congressional race.Raman moved to the United States with her family at the age of six. She graduated from Harvard University and earned a master's degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Before entering electoral politics, she worked on homelessness initiatives and co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition in Los Angeles.In 2020, Raman defeated incumbent David Ryu to win a seat on the Los Angeles City Council, becoming the first South Asian person elected to the council. She won re-election in 2024 and has focused on housing affordability, tenant protections, homelessness and climate policy. She also served as executive director of Time's Up Entertainment, an organisation addressing sexual harassment in Hollywood.Raman entered the mayoral race in February 2026, despite having previously endorsed Bass. She finished second in the June 2 primary, securing a place in the November runoff against the incumbent. Her campaign proposes increasing housing construction, strengthening renter protections, improving basic city services and expanding unarmed emergency-response services. She has also pledged to protect immigrants and streamline permits to support small businesses.Her campaign faces scrutiny over her changing positions on policing, homelessness programmes and the city's mansion tax. Bass and her supporters have questioned Raman's experience and approach to public safety, while Raman argues that Los Angeles needs a change in leadership and more accountable government.The contest will test whether Raman can turn her progressive support and record on housing into a citywide winning coalition against an incumbent backed by prominent Democrats and much of the City Council.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi air defences intercept Houthi barrage near Mecca
articles.summary: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalate as fierce ground battles and a devastating siege strangle Yemen’s Taiz.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition has intercepted a barrage of projectiles from Yemen that targeted cities across the kingdom.

Saudi Civil Defence said that shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles, suspected to have been fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, fell in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh, and Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca province.

A drone and ballistic missile were also intercepted over the Saudi capital Riyadh during the barrage, which began Saturday evening.

By midday Sunday, coalition forces had intercepted a cruise missile targeting Khamis Mushait, with warning sirens blaring out across Taif and Jazan. In total, 10 ballistic missiles directed at the southern region were intercepted.

Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi said the strikes represented “a grave violation of the sanctity of the Holy Sites and a provocation to the sentiments of Muslims worldwide”, referring to the interceptions in Mecca, home of the Kaaba and Masjid al-Haram. The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia group, have denied targeting Muslim holy sites in Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom has faced waves of Houthi missile and drone strikes in recent weeks, targeting civilian and military infrastructure.

Riyadh announced late Saturday that international flights from King Khalid International Airport would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.

This follows the suspension of flights from the Riyadh airport after waves of Houthi strikes, including one on October 10 that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.

Early Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned civilians away from the Saudi capital’s airport.

“King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is not safe because it is a military target, and we renew our warning to airlines, employees, and travelers,” Saree stated. He also announced seven operations targeting Saudi oil facilities and military bases.

Yemen has been in a state of war since Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south.

After a brief ceasefire, fighting in Yemen has intensified after government forces attacked Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation arriving from Tehran.

The Houthis then launched a surprise offensive in September, capturing Yemen’s western coast, including the city of Mocha.

Forces aligned with the internationally recognised government launched “Operation Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, aimed at retaking territories lost to the Houthis.

On Sunday, Yemen’s armed forces said the military had carried out 736 strikes on Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, leading to 307 people being “neutralised” and the destruction of 68 military vehicles.

Amid the military escalation, the Rasd Organization for Rights and Freedoms has warned of the dire humanitarian situation in the city of Taiz, which is under a Houthi siege.

“About 1,110 kidney failure patients face the risks of a shortage of dialysis supplies, given the need for about 120 dialysis sessions daily along with 192 patients in intensive care units and 154 children in incubators, due to the Houthi siege imposed on the city of Taiz since October 4,” the group said.

articles.title: Girl, four, dies after fall from tower block in Barking
articles.summary: Paramedics gave first aid at the scene on Saturday morningb ut the child later died, police say.
articles.body:
A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in East London.

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height.

Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.

A Met spokesperson said the incident was not believed to be suspicious.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said.

"An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious.

"We urge anyone with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 2424/24OCT."

articles.title: The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners
articles.summary: As Sudan’s war destroys livelihoods, the death of 16-year-old Altayeb Alhadi highlights dangers of artisanal mining.
articles.body:
When Altayeb Alhadi was just six years old, his father died after a well collapsed in his village in White Nile state, south-central Sudan. Two months later, and his mother also died, leaving the five children in the family as orphans. As the eldest of the siblings, it was Altayeb’s responsibility to find work and help the family survive.

At 14, he travelled hundreds of kilometres from his home in Galli village to seek work in the north, where gold mines dot the landscape, so he could feed his siblings and keep them in school.

“We warned him about the dangers, but he was ambitious. Some relatives were already working in the area although they had found jobs in restaurants and other services rather than underground extraction,” Ayateb’s uncle Alhadi Hamid told Al Jazeera.

The boy initially worked in transport and other jobs, but when he heard lucrative stories from miners in the area, he began to search for gold in the surrounding mountains.

Altayeb died in an air strike attributed to the Egyptian military at a gold-mining site near Jabal Al-Aigdat in Sudan’s Red Sea region on October 10, which killed at least 72 miners , a few months after he began working at the site.

“It was less than 30 minutes since we separated, and he said he was going to the mine. We suddenly heard a loud sound of bombardment, and we ran. It was too chaotic with people running in all directions and many attacks taking place within a few minutes,” a fellow miner told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“We found Altayeb with his hand and leg [blown off] and a severe injury to his abdomen [which] was open. We tried to help him and took him to a safer place near a mountain. We were terrified. He died within hours. … We couldn’t believe how quickly things could happen.”

Altayeb worked alongside about 15 young men and children, using basic tools to extract gold from the rocks. The miners worked night and day, taking the material they gathered to nearby mills for processing.

Proceeds from any gold found were shared, but earnings depended on the amount of gold recovered and individual agreements. On productive days, the group could earn more than $100, the miner said.

“We used to dig for two to three weeks until we found a gram or less. If the gold percentage in the well wasn’t good, we would change locations. When we found a gram or less, we sold it and shared the profit, which was about $100,” Altayeb’s former colleague said.

For young people supporting relatives, even irregular earnings in these dangerous gold mines can seem preferable to unemployment.

Altayeb told his siblings 10 days before his death that he would soon return home, his sister Rogaia Alhadi told local media.

Friends told the family that Altayeb visited them at a restaurant near the mining site on the morning of the attack, his uncle said. They shared a cup of tea before heading towards the mine for the final time. Minutes later, the air strike hit the area.

Authorities in Egypt have accused Sudanese miners of crossing its border and reportedly linked some to gold smuggling, drugs and human trafficking. The Sudanese side did not respond to these allegations.

Since a civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group broke out in 2023, the economy has tanked and forced thousands with no other source of income to find work in the artisanal gold mines of northern Sudan.

This can vary from independent prospecting to working in investor-owned pits for a share of the proceeds. Earnings depend on the amount of gold found, equipment and fuel costs, and profit percentages agreed with financiers.

Although some miners strike gold, they still face an array of dangers, ranging from collapsing shafts and unstable ground to air strikes. Limited medical care makes mining, particularly in remote areas, especially hazardous.

Living conditions are also extremely hard. Mohamed Awadalkarim, who was a miner in River Nile state for 10 years, said workers often shelter in makeshift huts made from burlap sacks and plastic sheeting. Their diet consists mainly of lentils and sorghum porridge.

But for families without reliable incomes, mining offers a possible source of immediate earnings. Miners may spend hours searching for gold and not find enough to cover their expenses. Others share proceeds with investors or equipment owners, leaving them with limited money left.

Artisanal and small-scale mining accounted for 53.71 tonnes, or about 83 per cent, of Sudan’s declared gold production in 2024, but this was just in areas under government control, according to research by the Chatham House think tank. About one million people were involved in artisanal mining across Sudan’s 18 states, generating $1bn annually for the country.

Artisanal mines, while generally viewed as being outside the main war-funding networks, have still been exposed to violence.

On June 16, several people were reportedly killed and injured in attacks on mining sites near the Egyptian border, according to local sources and miners.

The repeated air strikes near Sudan’s border with Egypt have raised concerns about civilian protection, territorial sovereignty and accountability.

Egyptian authorities have accused Sudanese prospectors of crossing the border to mine near a concession managed by an Egyptian company, but there is little independent evidence to back these claims.

Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan reportedly ordered a fact-finding committee involving prosecutors, judicial representatives and security agencies to investigate the attack. Findings from an inquiry into a similar incident announced in June have not been made public.

Altayeb paid the highest price in this regional conflict and the hunt for gold, which provides huge profits for some and meagre incomes for many.

Altayeb’s siblings are now living with their extended family, including uncles, aunts and cousins. People who know them are trying to help his brothers and sisters and are carrying out community initiatives in Galli to keep his memory alive.

“We will raise the children and care for them as he would have wanted. He was young, caring and brave, and he will always be remembered,” Altayeb said.
