articles.title: Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
articles.summary: Bangladesh expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but that’s not the complete economic picture.
articles.body:
Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s. But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.

The projected 2026 per capita GDP of Bangladesh, home to about 175 million people, is $2,886, compared with $2,749 in India as Dhaka emerges as one of South Asia’s notable economic success stories over the past two decades. Bangladesh’s economy is currently larger than that of Pakistan, from which Dhaka seceded in 1971.

Experts link the rise to the country’s $38bn garment industry, remittances and growing participation of women in the workforce.

But high inflation and slowing growth are now putting that progress under pressure. Meanwhile, the Indian economy is expected to grow by 7 percent this year, compared with 3.6 percent in Bangladesh.

So how should one read these numbers, and what do they really mean for millions of people living in these countries?

The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook report underscores differences in how the Indian and Bangladeshi economies are reacting to inflation and the economic pressures caused by two major wars that have jolted energy markets.

Bangladesh is expected to have a GDP of $506.4bn in 2026, compared with India’s $4.15 trillion. But its lead in GDP per capita reverses when adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. On this measure, India is projected to have a GDP per capita at $12,998, compared with Bangladesh’s $10,884.

PPP is an economic metric that represents what money can actually buy in different countries after adjusting for the cost of living. The figures mean that Indians have a higher buying capacity than Bangladeshis.

The IMF projected India’s average consumer-price inflation at 5 percent, compared with 8.7 percent in Bangladesh, pointing to greater cost-of-living pressures in Dhaka.

India is relatively wealthier than Bangladesh and is home to a big industrial base, including its significant technology sector.

India’s economy is expected to grow by 7 percent in 2026, nearly twice Bangladesh’s 3.6 percent rate.

For context, the average per capita GDP in developing economies is about $7,746 – and the global average is about $15,889 – against Bangladesh’s $2,886 and India’s $2,749.

Where are India’s and Bangladesh’s economies expected to go?

In the next year, the IMF report projected that Bangladesh’s per capita GDP would reach $3,219, still higher than India’s $3,036 – a difference, according to the estimates, that should continue marginally in 2028.

In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF.

Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s.

But GDP per capita alone does not paint a complete economic picture because it conceals inequalities in income and wealth distribution. The dollar-denominated figure also changes with the exchange rate, which means that a change in a currency’s value can alter the relative numbers without a change in economic output.

In brief, the growth in Bangladesh’s economy in the past two decades has focused on export-oriented manufacturing, particularly its ready-made garment industry, which has been a major source of export earnings and employment, in addition to remittances from Bangladeshis working abroad.

Meanwhile, India has a diversified economy, with services playing a major role alongside manufacturing and agriculture. Its domestic market, technology and business services, industrial base and consumer demand provide multiple sources of economic activity.

In both countries, however, economic growth over the past decade has been unequal with increasing concentration in wealthier households.

Is Bangladesh a South Asian success story?

To some extent, yes, analysts said while expressing caution about unequal growth.

Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian economist, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s economy has shown consistent economic growth of 6 percent per annum alongside a long-term decline in population growth.

The country has also seen its manufacturing contribution to gross value added shoot up from 16.6 percent in 2014 to 22 percent in 2025, Mehrotra said. On the other hand, World Bank data showed India’s manufacturing value added falling from 15.1 percent of GDP in 2014 to 13.5 percent in 2024.

“That’s a positive side of export-oriented manufacturing growth that Bangladesh is getting right,” he said.

However, the global energy shock from the United States-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, has jolted Bangladesh.

Bangladesh imports 95 percent of its oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and much of these imports comes from the Middle East.

The ready‑made garment industry, which accounts for more than 80 percent of Bangladesh’s export earnings, has also been hit as its shipment routes via the Red Sea and the Middle East have been disrupted.

articles.title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
articles.summary: The authorities had justified the ban by saying online content was fuelling conflict, while the opposition had condemned it as an abuse of power.
articles.body:
Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time.

The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment.

The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country.

The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure.

Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban.

The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.

Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions.

The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power.

Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family.

At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s pitch: Can Israel use crypto to evade economic sanctions?
articles.summary: Prime Minister Netanyahu mulls cryptocurrency as answer to economic sanctions on Israel, but there are few buyers.
articles.body:
Two days before the general elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel should prepare to use cryptocurrency to circumvent potential sanctions on the country amid growing global isolation over its genocidal war on Gaza and settlement expansions in the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu on Friday said that blockchain-based cryptocurrency is the solution to bypass the mounting economic sanctions that would keep the country out of the international financial system.

The Bank of Israel, the country’s central bank, rejected Netanyahu’s plan, and opposition parties said the incumbent prime minister’s vision is a recipe for disaster and increasing isolation.

So, can Israel really circumvent sanctions by dealing in crypto?

“We need to prepare ways to evade banking sanctions through an alternative economic system,” Netanyahu said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 10 last Friday.

“You know what that means – the currencies that can bypass them,” he said, adding that he was referring to blockchain-based crypto.

Netanyahu’s crypto pitch comes as Israel has been facing international isolation over its extreme policies against Palestinians: a surge in settler violence, anti-Palestinian rhetoric and the acceleration of illegal settlements in the occupied territories of the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Israel has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians since launching its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago. It has also been accused of committing war crimes in southern Lebanon, which has been hit almost daily by Israeli attacks despite a “ceasefire” now in place.

Israel has also carried out attacks on regional countries, including Iran, as part of its expansionist Greater Israel project , which is rooted in the biblical claim that Israel is entitled to the land between the Nile (in present-day Egypt) and the Euphrates (present-day Iraq).

Netanyahu has vowed to expand settlements, which are considered illegal under international laws, and has reiterated that he would not allow the formation of a Palestinian state, drawing condemnation from his European allies.

Last month, at least 12 major economies, including the United Kingdom, pledged coordinated measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The European Union has also sanctioned settlement-linked individuals and groups. Spain and the Republic of Ireland have introduced restrictions on settlement goods, while the Netherlands brought a broader ban on their import, purchase and sale into force in September.

Israel’s banking system has not yet been targeted by sanctions.

Moreover, Netanyahu also warned that Israel needs to look out for financing its own military, in the face of less support from Washington in bankrolling its wars – because “America has changed”.

“It [financing] will end. It is only a matter of time,” Netanyahu said, adding that after US President Donald Trump’s tenure ends in two years, Israel should prepare for a less favorable White House.

The United States funnels billions of dollars to the Israeli military annually, but the genocidal war on Gaza has changed unrestricted military support for Israel, which a growing number of Americans have started to question.

Netanyahu also faces an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes, while the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is hearing the case of genocide against Israel brought by South Africa.

If the ICJ verdict goes against Israel, it would further intensify calls for sanctions against the country, including restrictions on arms exports, trade and financial ties, as governments around the world face mounting pressure to hold Israeli officials accountable.

If Israeli banks are restricted from international transfers, then businesses could attempt to pay overseas suppliers using cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, stablecoins, or other digital assets.

Cryptocurrency is digital money, transferred between people or businesses over the internet, where transactions are recorded on a digital ledger called a blockchain. Public blockchains can transfer assets directly between digital wallets without a bank processing every transaction.

Sanctioned actors have used cryptocurrencies for cross-border payments, including transactions connected to oil sales and procurement. Russia, which has been slapped with sanctions for its invasion of Ukraine, has reportedly used cryptocurrencies to make some payments to evade sanctions.

But crypto cannot replace conventional banking at the scale of today’s economy. It can be a parallel medium, but cannot replace the traditional banking system, experts note.

Moreover, crypto does not solve a fundamental problem that Israel faces from sanctions: financial isolation, which by design also demoralises investors and businesses. It also restricts access to financial institutions or penalises third parties that deal with designated entities. Therefore, even if a business uses crypto for payments, the transaction would still be illegal.

Israel’s economy also depends on international trade and technology supply chains, wherein its defence and tech industry need foreign components and specialist equipment.

More than 100 experts and former Israeli officials, in a statement issued on Sunday, expressed “grave concern and anxiety” over Netanyahu’s crypto plan.

They accused the Israeli prime minister of failing to grasp the seriousness of the threat, and criticised his proposal as a solution more commonly associated with criminal organisations.

Sanctions would cause “enormous and irreversible damage” to the Israeli economy, they said.

The Bank of Israel rejected Netanyahu’s plan, arguing that cryptocurrencies “cannot be used as a route for bypassing sanctions”.

“The right thing for Israel’s economy is preserving the economic relationships with our principal trade partners and focusing on preventing sanctions and their negative influence on the economy,” the central bank said in a statement. “This issue is within the responsibilities of the political echelon, and it should act to advance it.”

However, Netanyahu responded by saying that he is grateful for the bank’s advice, “But I do what I think [is best].”

Netanyahu’s main opponent, Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, said that the PM’s vision “is a threat to national security”.

“After he finished dismantling Israeli society and weakening the [Israeli military], Netanyahu has marked the next target: the dismantling of the Israeli economy for generations ahead,” he said.

Eisenkot further said that the prime minister has “lost touch with reality” — referring to the crypto-based solution “to the nadir in international [relations] that he himself brought upon us — to disconnect Israel from the global economy.”

Taking a dig at the gaps in the approach, Eisenkot said he wondered, “How will Google buy an Israeli company on the condition that it bypass an international bank and pay in crypto?”

articles.title: In 1961, a Joan Eardley painting left a Scottish gallery and vanished into private hands; 64 years later, it surfaced in an English charity shop, before selling for £29,500 in 2026 to fund medical research
articles.summary: A landscape painting by Scottish artist Joan Eardley, which disappeared into private ownership after leaving a Scottish gallery in 1961, has been found in
articles.body: A landscape painting by Scottish artist Joan Eardley, which disappeared into private ownership after leaving a Scottish gallery in 1961, has been found in an English charity shop. The painting later sold for £29,500, with all the money going towards medical research in the UK. The oil painting, titled Summer Fields, was found when a charity shop manager in the East Midlands accepted a dark canvas as part of a house clearance donation. A damaged paper label on the back of the frame offered a clue. It read: “Summer, Joan, Exhibited, The Scottish Gallery.” The shop staff contacted The Scottish Gallery in Edinburgh. A search of its historical records confirmed the painting's identity, 64 years after it was first sold.Uncovering the paper trailAfter receiving the enquiry from the East Midlands charity shop, Tommy Zyw, director of The Scottish Gallery, checked the gallery's handwritten sales books and old daily records. The records showed that Summer Fields was first sold by Joan Eardley in May 1961. After confirming the details, gallery staff arranged for the painting to be safely taken back to Edinburgh for a closer inspection. "From the moment it was unwrapped, its authenticity was clear," Zyw stated in details published by art and events website What's On Edinburgh. "The surface, the handling, the authority of the mark all pointed unmistakably to Eardley. Sixty-four years after it had left us, Summer Fields had returned." Professional cleaning removed years of dirt from the canvas. This revealed a view of the coastal village of Catterline in Aberdeenshire in late September. Eardley lived and painted there during the final years of her life. The painting shows part of a farmer's field in the autumn light. Wild grasses and seed heads fill the foreground, giving the scene a rich texture.Raising funds for medical researchThe painting returned to public view when The Scottish Gallery displayed it at the British Art Fair in September 2025. It was later shown at the gallery's main premises on Dundas Street in Edinburgh. The artwork was then sold on behalf of the East Midlands charity shop to a prominent private collector of Scottish art. The sale raised £29,500, making it the most valuable single item the charity had ever sold. All the proceeds went directly towards medical research across the United Kingdom. Speaking about the painting's journey, Zyw said: “This story speaks of the enduring power of Joan Eardley's painting and of the role of careful stewardship, archives, and expertise in bringing such works back into the public arena.”He added: “From Joan Eardley painting this work in Catterline, its sale in 1961, decades enjoyed privately then its arrival on the charity shop's shelf, to the phone call that started its return to Scotland; we have been proud to support Summer Fields on its continuing journey.”Public exhibition and lasting legacyThe return of Summer Fields comes as the National Galleries of Scotland presents a major exhibition of Eardley's work. Titled Joan Eardley | The Nature of Painting, it is being held at Modern Two in Edinburgh. The exhibition runs from 2 April to 28 June 2026. It features more than 30 works by Eardley, alongside selected pieces from the national collection. The display explores her work and links with Scottish and international artists of her time. Eardley died of cancer in 1963 at the age of 42. She is still regarded as one of the most expressive British painters of the mid-20th century. Much of her work focused on children living in Glasgow's Townhead district and the changing weather along the Kincardineshire coast. The Scottish Gallery has represented Eardley's estate since it first exhibited her paintings in 1955. It has continued to arrange private sales and help place her works with collectors. The discovery of Summer Fields has brought an important part of Eardley's artistic history back into view. Its sale has also raised £29,500 for medical research across the UK.You use AI every day. articles.title: Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
articles.summary: Serbia is heading to the polls as a student movement attempts to oust longtime populist leader Aleksandar Vučić.
articles.body:
Early reports suggest Serbian voters have turned out in large numbers for its parliamentary election, as a student protest movement attempts to end the rule of the country's right-wing populist leader.

Preliminary reports suggest a record high turnout, with 46% having cast their vote by 14:00 local time (13:00 GMT), nearly a million more than the comparable figure for the previous election in December 2023.

The apparent high turnout is fuelling the hopes of opposition party Student List that they can oust Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), who have been in power since 2012.

The snap elections called by Vučić follow two years of student protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.

Anti-corruption movement Student List are running on a manifesto including purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists heading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.

Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.

What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election

Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election

Most commentators suggest that a high final turnout, 65% or above, would favour the students.

Voting ends at 20:00, with first indications of results expected two hours later.

Long queues formed outside polling stations in larger cities and smaller towns alike in Serbia, and at polling stations abroad - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles and Chicago. In Paris, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain.

Tensions are high across Serbia. In Belgrade, police have closed streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK).

In the street nearby, cars at the traffic lights lowered their windows to blast one of the students' anthems from loudspeakers, 'I want three kisses' - a folk song favoured because the Students' List is number three on the ballot paper. Young people on the pavement nearby started dancing.

Vučić and his SNS party are number one on the ballot paper. He has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.

Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.

SNS posters plastered around cities show two hands clasped together in solidarity: the hands of doctors and nurses, farmers, construction workers, teachers and parents.

"These are the hands that hold Serbia in their palms," says Vučić in his campaign video. "And with these hands, calmly and with dignity, we shall finish what we started."

That is question of this election, continuity or change.

Amid fears of electoral fraud by the SNS, the students have delegated at least two observers to each of Serbia's 8,210 voting stations.

Videos circulating on social media on Sunday morning show a cafe in the southern city of Nis, where ballot papers were allegedly filled out in advance in a practice known as 'chain voting'. Signs in the window read "private party". When they realise that they are being filmed, the papers are quickly hidden.

There have also been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists at several polling stations.

"We are witnessing a unique experiment in European contemporary history," Žarko Korać, a former deputy prime minister and long-term opponent of nationalist parties in Serbia including the SNS, told the BBC.

Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Ilija Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.

The Student List of candidates for parliament also includes doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities

"These are people that don't know each other, you have no idea what their political beliefs are, and we now expect them to create a functioning government. So it's anybody's guess what happens after they win," Korać says.

"On the other hand, if Vučić declares victory this evening, probably late in the evening, I don't think the students will accept that."

Korać suggests that many former Vučić loyalists in high office could change sides at the last moment, if the students win. A close result, however, with both sides claiming victory, could result in weeks or months of political instability.

The electorate is 6.45 million in a population of 6.53 million, raising concerns about the reliability of the electoral register. Serbs from Kosovo, and dual Serbian citizens from neighbouring Bosnia also have the right to vote.

Katarina, 29, told the BBC she had travelled from the Netherlands back home to Serbia to vote for Student List, even though she could have cast her ballot remotely.

"I wanted to be a part of this, and I wanted to be part of a movement," she told the BBC outside a polling station in the capital's Zvezdara district.

"I think they have a chance of winning," she said, but expressed doubt about whether such a result would be respected by Vučić.

Asked whether the party's selection of candidates from different walks of life might hinder its ability to govern, she responded: "Just because they're politically inexperienced, they are experts in their own fields, which we have not seen thus far."

articles.title: Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
articles.summary: Jordan’s prime minister represents king at funeral for eight of the church attack victims as hunt for gunmen continues.
articles.body:
Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance.

The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there.

Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning.

The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency.

Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard.

Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra.

Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said.

Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed.

When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded.

“Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me,” she recalled calling to him. He briefly opened his eyes before dying, she said.

Father Yohanna Hamati told AFP that about 170 to 200 people were at the church for Friday’s funeral when firing began outside.

The mourners initially struggled to understand what was happening, he said, before people began rushing into the church to escape.

By Saturday, bullet holes remained in the walls and wooden pews, and windows had been shattered.

Church workers were cleaning away blood as villagers prepared to bury the dead. Jordanian authorities have described the attack as “extremist terrorism”.

King Abdullah, who visited some of the wounded in hospital on Friday, has promised a forceful response and the assailants are still being sought.

Officials say they have not established whether the attackers were connected to an armed group and no organisation has claimed responsibility.

The violence has also drawn expressions of solidarity across religious lines. Christians account for about 3 percent of Jordan’s largely Muslim population and AFP reported that Muslims were among those wounded.

Young volunteers visited a hospital in Karak with flowers and a message reading, “Our loss is one”.

The mourning reached Washington, DC, on Sunday, where members of the Jordanian community lit candles outside their country’s embassy.

Jordan’s ambassador to the US, Dina Kawar, told those gathered that efforts to stir religious division were “bound to fail”. Back in Hamoud, Father Hamati appealed for unity, stressing that Muslims had also suffered in the attack.

“We make no distinction between Muslim and Christian,” he told AFP.

articles.title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
articles.summary: He will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", authorities said.
articles.body:
A man suspected of a deadly gun attack near Paris has left custody and been placed under psychiatric observation, French anti-terrorism officials have said.

One person was killed and five others injured on Friday when an attacker opened fire from his car - first in Trappes, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin.

The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said.

President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack", adding that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion.

It marked a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation", the French president said.

PNAT said the move to place the suspect under psychiatric evaluation followed guidance from a psychiatric expert.

The evaluation will determine whether the suspect should remain in police custody and is "likely to last 48 hours", PNAT added.

PNAT said the suspect was also found to have cannabis and cocaine in his bloodstream.

French newspaper Le Monde and news agency AFP report that a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf were found at the suspect's home, citing a source close to the investigation.

The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".

He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.

Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.

The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up.

"His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts."

Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.

The mayor of La Verrière, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better".

Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.

The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".

He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

articles.title: After decades of abandonment, 48 acres once home to Ohio's SeaWorld and Six Flags parks are set to reopen on October 25, with a restored pier and historic gatehouses marking the first phase of Aurora Park
articles.summary: After years of lying abandoned, a 48-acre site in Ohio that was once home to SeaWorld and Six Flags amusement parks is opening to the public again, but
articles.body: After years of lying abandoned, a 48-acre site in Ohio that was once home to SeaWorld and Six Flags amusement parks is opening to the public again, but this time as a recreation space rather than an entertainment destination filled with rides and attractions that it once used to be. Aurora Park at Geauga Lake is opening its first section on October 25, bringing visitors back to a property that was once a popular family destination in Northeast Ohio, with a restored pier, historic gatehouse pavilions and landscaped lawns forming part of the new park.The city acquired the lakefront property in December 2024 for $5.3 million, several years after the last attraction on the site, Wildwater Kingdom, closed in 2016. Since then, plans have been underway to make the lakefront accessible to the public again, with the first phase focusing on outdoor recreation and the restoration of some structures from the site's amusement park years. A playground, public beach and other recreational facilities are expected to follow in later phases.What visitors can expect at Aurora ParkThe first phase of the project focuses on making the lakefront accessible to the public again, with seating and picnic areas, restrooms, boating access and a pier offering views of Geauga Lake. According to News 5 Cleveland, the initial nine-acre section also includes kayak and boat access ramps, while the restored structures and preserved objects from the site's amusement park years are set to provide a nostalgic reminder of its earlier identity.Some of these features are particularly significant for visitors who remember their childhood days at the park and its attractions. The two former SeaWorld gatehouse pavilions have been restored, and memorabilia from the Geauga Lake amusement park years is being incorporated into the new public space. The city is also planning an accessible play area for a subsequent phase, while future development could include a public beach, a pool house, sports facilities and an amphitheatre.However, the reopening does not mean that the former amusement park rides or SeaWorld's marine animal shows are returning. Instead, the redevelopment is intended to create a community space where people can enjoy the lake, take part in outdoor activities and revisit a location that holds memories for many residents of Northeast Ohio.From SeaWorld Ohio to Six Flags: The site's historyThe property has a long history as an entertainment destination for local families, with Geauga Lake becoming a popular amusement destination long before the modern theme parks that later occupied the surrounding land were developed. SeaWorld Ohio opened on the lakefront in 1970, bringing marine animal attractions and shows to the area before the two attractions became part of a larger amusement park operation.According to Spectrum News 1's report on the redevelopment, the area was home to several attractions over more than a century, including Geauga Lake, SeaWorld and Wildwater Kingdom. SeaWorld closed in 2000, and the site subsequently became part of Six Flags Worlds of Adventure. The wider amusement park property later passed through different ownership, with Geauga Lake's rides eventually shutting down in 2007.Wildwater Kingdom, the last amusement attraction operating on the site, closed in 2016, leaving the property vacant and inaccessible to the public. Its closure marked the end of an era for a location that had once drawn families to the lakefront.Why Aurora bought the abandoned lakefront propertyThe move to transform the property into a public park followed years of planning and discussions about the future of the lakefront. In its 2024 Year in Review, the City of Aurora described acquiring Geauga Lake and the adjacent land as a way to preserve public access to the water and develop a recreation space for future generations.The city completed the purchase on December 20, 2024, acquiring the lake and approximately 48 acres of surrounding lakefront property for $5.3 million, according to News 5 Cleveland. The acquisition was intended to protect the lakefront from other forms of development while giving residents and visitors an opportunity to enjoy the natural surroundings.Construction on the site began in 2026 after planning and design work, with a $12 million bond helping finance the first phase of redevelopment. The project is being developed in stages, allowing the city to make the property accessible while continuing work on additional facilities in later phases.A beach and playground are planned for future phasesThe opening of Aurora Park represents only the beginning of the city's plans for the property, with additional recreational facilities expected to be developed over the coming years. As reported by Spectrum News 1, the next phase is expected to include a large playground, while a public beach and pool house are planned for a later stage, potentially by 2028.Other proposals include converting the former wave pool into a regular swimming pool, along with sports courts, playing fields, a climbing area and an amphitheatre. These facilities are part of a broader vision to make the lakefront useful to the community beyond the opening of the first section.For now, the restored pier, lawns and gatehouses mark the return of public access to a property that spent years standing largely unused. While Aurora Park will look different from the amusement parks that once occupied the site, the redevelopment offers the city a chance to preserve a piece of local history while creating a new place for families to gather and enjoy Geauga Lake.You use AI every day. articles.body: Kolkata: The debate over the accusations made by veteran Naseeruddin Shah against the SRFTI administration refused to die down on Sunday. However, no one has taken onus or been identified for writing the slogans.Students addressed the media, where they called for halting saffronisation, privatisation, militarisation, and surveillance of educational campuses while ensuring student safety, democratic spaces, and regular student union elections. Those criticising the administration should first get verified information about the charges against Shubham before supporting him,” Kumar said.On Sunday, Chauhan reacted to Shah’s description of BJP as a “bloody jhooti party”. “A party that has been in the office for the last 12-13 years, you called it a ‘bloody jhooti party’. This should not be a part of the larger democratic process. I urge govt and the people concerned to look into it immediately and make sure that the students remain safe and a creative environment is created for them,” Behl said. articles.title: ‘Nothing new after Steve Jobs’: Billionaire Peter Thiel takes a brutal dig at Apple and Tim Cook
articles.summary: PayPal cofounder and billionaire investor Peter Thiel isn't holding back on his thoughts regarding Apple.
articles.body: PayPal cofounder and billionaire investor Peter Thiel isn't holding back on his thoughts regarding Apple. In a conversation with author Walter Isaacson on The Builders podcast, the venture capitalist argued that the tech giant hasn't brought anything genuinely groundbreaking to the table since Steve Jobs passed away in 2011.While acknowledging that Apple remains a powerhouse financially, Thiel made a clear distinction between raw corporate profit and true technological innovation."Nothing New After Jobs"During the interview, Thiel reflected on Apple's trajectory over the past decade and a half, suggesting that the company has mostly been riding the momentum of the original 2007 iPhone launch rather than inventing the next big thing."In my telling, it did nothing new after Jobs," Thiel said during the recording. "It turned out, yeah, the mobile phone was this giant invention - there was not that much more to do. Then it was just scaling and branding and building it out over 15 years or whatever."Since Jobs introduced the original iPhone, Apple has certainly broadened its ecosystem - expanding lines like the MacBook, iPad, and AirPods into everyday household devices. More recently, the company even stepped into new hardware territory with the release of its first foldable handset, the iPhone Duo. However, from Thiel's perspective, polishing and scaling existing form factors isn't the same as creating a whole new category.The company has also taken heat from critics over its broader software strategy, particularly as rival artificial intelligence tools from startups like OpenAI and Anthropic continue to capture public attention. Still, despite those critiques, Apple's hardware ecosystem remains a dominant force in consumer tech across the globe.Comparing Tim Cook with Elon Musk and Steve JobsThiel was careful to clarify that he doesn't consider Apple a failing company. In fact, he described it as a "pure, well-run value stock." His real issue lies in what he views as a shift away from the bold, risk-heavy innovation that defined its early years.Comparing corporate leadership styles, Thiel openly expressed his preference for visionaries over operational managers. "I would still say somehow Elon or Steve Jobs are way better for society than Tim Cook," he remarked, contrasting Apple's current CEO with its late cofounder and Tesla's chief executive.This isn't the first time Thiel has voiced skepticism about the tech giant's trajectory. articles.title: Opposition leader Machado returns to Venezuela from exile
articles.summary: After more than 10 months in exile, Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado has returned home to a political landscape that has been reshaped by her ally the United States without her involvement.
articles.body: After more than 10 months in exile, Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado has returned home to a political landscape that has been reshaped by her ally the United States without her involvement. “I am here. With you,” Machado announced on X Sunday morning shortly before other members of the opposition confirmed her arrival without providing details. She left Venezuela in December for Norway to accept the Nobel Peace Prize, which she was awarded for promoting democratic rights in her country. A month after she left, the US toppled her rival, strongman President Nicolás Maduro, and began working with the acting Venezuelan government to steer the country toward a democratic transition and political reconciliation. The process has involved several high-profile opposition figures but has excluded Machado and her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González Urrutia. Machado had repeatedly vowed to return home and hinted that she would run for president again if an election were held. In late August, a key member of her inner circle, Omar González, returned to the country after almost three years in exile, in what he called a “prelude” to Machado’s own arrival. Machado had attempted to re-enter Venezuela seven times over the past few months without success, according to her advisers. She first tried in late June to help with reconstruction efforts after two powerful earthquakes devastated the country, but claimed the government thwarted her return by closing its airspace. She tried again in late September while acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, but she was denied entry three times in a single day. During her more than 10 months away, Machado traveled the world to rally political support from her allies, including US President Donald Trump, to whom she gifted her Nobel Prize. While the Trump administration has shown support for Machado in the past, it has largely sidelined her from Venezuela’s ongoing political transition. After ousting Maduro in January, Trump called Machado a “very nice woman,” but claimed she “does not have the support or the respect within the country” to be leader. Instead, the US has been working with Maduro’s successor, Delcy Rodríguez, to enact political and economic reforms in the country. Rodríguez has met just about every demand from the Trump administration, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country. In late August, Trump announced that the US had reached an agreement to take majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela, a move some consider beneficial for both the US oil industry and the Venezuelan economy. Machado in a video statement questioned why the oil agreement announced by Trump was being signed by the Venezuelan government, which she called an “illegitimate regime.” The government clung to power in 2024 after state-controlled electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner of the last presidential election, despite experts concluding that such a result was statistically improbable. Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly vowed that Venezuela would hold new elections and transition to a full democracy, which the US says is the main goal, but the acting government has yet to announce when a vote will take place. Trump has repeatedly said the country is not ready for elections yet but has insisted that a lot of progress has been made.

articles.title: Bus crash in Kenya kills 22 near the site of a previous fatal accident
articles.summary: MAKUENI, Kenya — A bus collided with a truck on Kenya’s main highway on Sunday, killing at least 22 people, police said.
articles.body: MAKUENI, Kenya — A bus collided with a truck on Kenya’s main highway on Sunday, killing at least 22 people, police said. The crash came three weeks after 17 people died in another accident along the same highway linking the capital, Nairobi, with the coastal city of Mombasa. Some 24 others were injured in the Sunday morning crash and were receiving treatment, according to Paul Kisienya, the medical superintendent at Mtito Andei hospital that received most of those injured. The passengers were returning to Mombasa after attending the funeral of their church pastor in western Kenya when the accident occurred. A mother of two, Violet Mwandonyi, said the bus had just left Mtito Andei town, where the passengers had eaten breakfast. “I cannot recall what exactly happened. The last thing I remember is that we were all wailing and calling on motorists to come to our rescue. I don’t know the fate of my two children who were on the bus,” she said. The circumstances remain unclear but a passenger, Spenza Mudave said a truck hit the bus from behind, causing the bus to roll. The National Transport Safety Authority had suspected that this was a case of “improper overtaking” due to the information gathered that the vehicles collided head-on. Speeding and poor road conditions have previously been cited as contributing factors in road accidents in Kenya.

articles.title: Row over construction of forest office in Palakkad
articles.summary: Controversy over NABARD-funded Eastern Circle forest office building in Palakkad as NGO seeks probe into plan changes, record room demolition, and alleged irregularities.
articles.body: Kochi: A controversy has erupted over the construction of Eastern Circle office building in Palakkad and the decision to demolish record rooms keeping documents.NGO ANEC Trust has filed an urgent petition seeking an independent inquiry into alleged procedural, financial and administrative irregularities in the construction of the Eastern Circle office building at Aranyabhavan in Olavakkode, Palakkad, funded by NABARD.The petition, submitted to L Chandrasekhar, additional principal chief conservator of forests (forest management, finance, budget and allotment) at the forest headquarters in Thiruvananthapuram, raises concerns over a proposal to accommodate the wildlife circle office in a building sanctioned for the Eastern Circle 0ffice and the custodian of vested forests.According to ANEC Trust, the approved plan includes dedicated record rooms, a conference hall and other essential facilities. It has sought clarification on whether the proposed change in the Eastern Circle office building’s intended use has received prior written approval from the govt and NABARD.The petition also alleges that the contractor was verbally instructed to demolish or modify completed record rooms to facilitate the proposed changes. ANEC Trust has urged the authorities to suspend any such work until the original project sanction, approved plans, estimates and relevant permissions are verified.The record rooms are intended to house more than 3,000 old and ongoing case files and vested forest records, including documents relating to litigation dating back to 1974 before forest tribunals and Kerala High Court and Supreme Court. The trust warned that inadequate storage could jeopardise document security and affect ongoing legal proceedings.The petition further calls for scrutiny of a potential conflict of interest, citing reports that the heads of Eastern Circle and Wildlife Circle are spouses. It has sought verification of compliance with applicable service rules and administrative procedures, without prejudging the officials’ responsibility.The trust has also urged an objective assessment of office-space requirements and available alternatives, including space that may become available following the relocation of the Working Plan Division.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Israel is holding its most important election in years. Here’s what’s at stake
articles.summary: When Israelis go the polls on October 27, they will face a familiar question: Should Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, stay in power?
articles.body: When Israelis go the polls on October 27, they will face a familiar question: Should Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, stay in power? Nearly every recent election has been a referendum on Netanyahu. This time, many Israelis say the choice is more consequential than ever: not only about who will lead the country, but about where it is heading. It is the first national vote since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, the deadliest security failure in Israel’s history, and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, which have mobilized much of the country and subsequently deepened Israel’s international isolation. For many voters, this is the first chance to pass judgment on the leadership that presided over October 7 failures, to decide who should lead the country in conflict and who should carry the burden of increased military service. Netanyahu’s outgoing government – the first in decades to conclude a full four-year term – relied on far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners, who pushed Israel in a more nationalist and religious direction than ever before. He became the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial on corruption charges as his government pursued a judicial overhaul aimed at weakening the supreme court and other checks on power. The overhaul effort sparked massive protests in 2023. At stake in Tuesday’s election is whether Israel keeps moving in the nationalistic, conservative and religious direction – or changes course. The answer might not be clear for weeks, because of the way Israeli coalitions are built. Polls suggest neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is likely to win a majority alone, meaning the vote may launch Israel’s next political crisis rather than settle it. Who is running and who is ahead? Israelis vote for party lists, not individual candidates. In a society divided by nationality, religion, ethnicity and ideology, that produces a crowded field. Dozens of lists register each cycle – 37 this time around – but only those that pass a 3.25% vote threshold win seats and enter the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Polls suggest 11 to 13 parties will meet the bar; seats are allocated through a proportional representation system. The two largest parties are Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and Yashar, a new centrist party led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who has emerged as his principal challenger. The latest Channel 12 opinion poll puts Eisenkot first with 23 seats, ahead of the Likud with 21, though other pollsters differ. On the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, Likud is projected to take 30 seats and Eisenkot about 20. In head-to-head matchups about who is better suited to be prime minister, Eisenkot has led Netanyahu by a steady margin. But coming out as the largest party is not enough to win. A prime minister needs 61 seats to form a government, and no party has ever won that majority alone. So, election night usually settles very little. The real contest is the coalition calculus that follows, which can take days, weeks, and even months. Most polls put Netanyahu’s bloc, made up of Likud, two far-right parties led by Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, and two ultra-Orthodox parties, at 49 to 55 seats, short of the 61-seat majority. The opposition, which looks strong on paper, is deeply fragmented: Eisenkot has parties led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman to his right, and the Democrats party led by Yair Golan on his left. Bennett and Liberman have not endorsed Eisenkot and both have their own premiership aspirations. According to the opinion polls, any alternative government would probably need the support or the abstention of the Arab parties, and several opposition leaders have ruled out any cooperation. With no side holding a clear majority, a deadlock, a minority government, a unity government – or another election – are all plausible outcomes. What could swing the result? With neither bloc projected to win comfortably, the outcome may hinge on the margins: which small parties clear the 3.25% threshold and how many votes go to parties that miss it, effectively sending them down the drain. Turnout matters, since a few thousand votes can determine whether a party disappears entirely or enters parliament, or even becomes the kingmaker that breaks the deadlock between the blocs and reshapes the political map. Arab voter turnout could be pivotal. Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up roughly 20% of the Israeli population – have traditionally voted at lower rates than the national average. In the 2022 election, the Arab turnout was 53.2%, while the general turnout was 70.6%. This time, pollsters expect it to exceed 60%. That would raise the threshold and make it harder for small parties to survive. Netanyahu’s coalition has several small parties at potential risk, including Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and a new right- wing party led by Ofer Winter, a prominent retired military general. While most opposition parties sit safely above the line, another new, uncommitted small party, connecting a reservist and economic agenda, is polling close to the 3.25% threshold. Another factor drawing attention is Israelis living abroad. Israel does not allow overseas voting, except for diplomatic staff, and official data suggests more than 11% of the 7.3 million eligible voters, about 810,000 people, live outside the country. Thousands plan to fly to Israel to vote in person, a number that could potentially impact the election. What do Israelis vote about? In a country that has been through years of war, security and accountability are powerful electoral forces. But opinion polls suggest the cost of living is also a leading concern for many voters – particularly for younger ones. According to the latest Channel 12 poll, 21% of Israelis rank the economy and the cost of living as their top priority in the coming election – ahead of the ultra-Orthodox conscription with 17%, the October 7 failure at 14% and the war with Iran at 10%. The picture differs sharply by political bloc: among voters of Netanyahu’s coalition – the war with Iran ranks first at 21%, while among opposition voters, the October 7 failure leads at 28%. A September survey by the Achord research center at Hebrew University found that 58% of voters aged 22-34 year olds said cost of living and housing prices would drive their vote, while 36% cited security issues. Despite these figures, the economy has not been a central theme in the campaign topic – until this weekend, when Netanyahu moved it to the top of the agenda. In an interview to Channel 10 focused on the economy, Netanyahu addressed the wave of international condemnation of Israeli settlements in the West Bank and said Israel should prepare for possible international banking sanctions by developing “an economy that can circumvent them.” He said crypto currency and blockchain are being considered, and he had requested a plan to deal with it. The interview sparked harsh criticism of Netanyahu by economists, including a rare rebuke from the Bank of Israel, who publicly rejected the idea, which said that “cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means of circumventing sanctions.” Netanyahu’s main rivals portrayed his proposal as evidence he expects Israel to become more isolated. Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger, mocked the idea as “BibiCoin” and called it a “threat to national security,” accusing Netanyahu of planning to “dismantle the Israeli economy for generations ahead.” How might October 7 and the war in Gaza shape the vote? Netanyahu built his political career as a security hawk, yet he was prime minister on October 7, when Hamas infiltrated the Israeli border, killing more than 1,200 Israelis and taking 251 hostages into Gaza. He has resisted taking personal responsibility and has rejected demands to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures. His opponents have made that lack of accountability a central campaign theme. The war has also shaped Eisenkot’s personal story. His son Gal, 25, was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023, a loss that reinforces his appeal to voters focused on security. Other party lists have recruited bereaved families and relatives of former Israeli hostages as candidates. Opposition parties have also added new reservist candidates, fresh from fighting in Gaza and Lebanon, pushing the issue of military service to the top of the election agenda. Most Jewish Israelis over 18 are subject to conscription, but ultra-Orthodox men have long enjoyed a blanket exemption for religious study. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox coalition partners have sought to preserve and expand the exemption, even as the Israeli military says it is missing more than 12,000 personnel while being stretched by multi-front fighting. Reservists fill the gap, serving up to hundreds of days a year on repeated deployments. All the opposition parties have made universal service a central campaign pledge. What does the election mean for the Palestinians? The outgoing government was among the most hardline on Palestinian issues in Israel’s history, driven largely by two far-right nationalist party leaders. Smotrich, the finance minister, who also oversees civil administration in the occupied West Bank, pushed to expand settlements dramatically, while withholding tax revenues to the Palestinian Authority (PA), which critics say could bring its economic collapse. Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, championed a death penalty law in the Knesset, toughened conditions for Palestinian prisoners, and weakened police enforcement against Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Both opposed ending the Gaza war, both are advocating for Israeli settlements in Gaza, and both envision full annexation of and Jewish control over the West Bank. If Netanyahu returns to power with his current partners, that approach is likely to continue and intensify. Smotrich wants to cancel the Oslo Accords, dismantle the Palestinian Authority, and go to war in the West Bank. Ben-Gvir, who has said he will demand the defense ministry in a new government, has called for Palestinian emigration from Gaza and the West Bank. An opposition government would probably not represent a radical ideological reversal, and would change the tone more than the substance. Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has rejected Palestinian statehood, and any opposition coalition would include right-wing parties resistant to any concession. Still, a government not dependent on Ben- Gvir and Smotrich would likely act more forcefully against settler violence, drop open advocacy of emigration and PA collapse, and be more responsive and receptive to US and regional initiatives in Gaza and elsewhere. But it would inherit the same unresolved questions: how to disarm Hamas, who rebuilds Gaza, and who restores law and order in the West Bank. What does it mean for the rest of the world? The wars in Gaza and Lebanon, the conflict with Iran and the surge in settler violence have left Israel’s diplomatic standing at its weakest point in decades. Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court warrant alleging war crimes in Gaza, and he avoids traveling to most European countries because of the risk of being arrested. US President Donald Trump endorsed him ahead of the vote, but the picture in the wider American public is much less friendly. A March 2026 Pew Research Center poll found 60% of US adults surveyed held an unfavorable view of Israel, and 59% had little or no confidence in Netanyahu to do the right thing regarding global affairs. Pew’s Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey pointed the same way, with majorities in most of the 36 countries it covered holding unfavorable views of Israel and its prime minister. The shift has been sharpest in Western Europe, where several countries – including the United Kingdom, France and Canada – have recognized a Palestinian state and imposed sanctions and trade restrictions on Israeli settlements and individuals and entities linked to settler violence. Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have been personally sanctioned and are facing travel bans from multiple Western countries. If Netanyahu’s government is re-elected, that international pressure will likely grow. A government led by Eisenkot or another opposition figure might see some easing of tensions, at least at first. Firmer action on settler violence could open a window to restore warmer ties with some European governments and the US Democratic party. But it is not likely to reverse the broader trend. The main opposition contenders are not expected to overhaul Israel’s security and foreign policy, so a new government would regain some diplomatic breathing room, but not a clean slate.
